newsitem.title: USA: Intertie rating may hinge on Calif. load tripping.
newsitem.headline: Intertie rating may hinge on Calif. load tripping.

text.p: An increase in springtime capacity for the Pacific Intertie power transmission system may hinge on discussions about directly tripping loads in southern California, some industry sources said this week.
"People in the desert Southwest feel very strongly that direct load-tripping needs to be in place," said Jan Packwood, chairman of the Western Systems Coordinating Council (WSCC).
Direct load tripping is the practice of identifying ahead of time large end-users which automatically would be cut off from the power grid during an emergency.
Currently, California utilities conduct random load-shedding if voltage support problems reach critical levels, as they did during widespread blackouts last summer.

But Vikram Budhraja, Southern California Edison Co's vice president of system planning and operations, said California utilities have designed systems with enough redundancy to manage outages without impacting loads.
The direct load shedding being discussed would "add another layer of remedial action," he said.

"The WSCC needs to decide from a policy standpoint whether we manage the system to avoid shedding load or whether we manage the system for greater usage, but allow for direct-load tripping," Budhraja said.
In any case, it does not make sense to put only California customers at risk, and any provisions for direct load tripping would need to apply to the entire WSCC, he noted.
Budhraja said the issue is not crucial to further Intertie capacity increases, and the decision on whether to revise the transmission rating should be based solely on technical assessments of safety.
Intertie lines have been capped at 5,200 megawatts (MW), out of a rated capacity of 7,900 MW, since last August after the two blackouts.
WSCC chairman Packwood also said direct load tripping would be problematic, but could result in faster restoration of electricity service in the event of another blackout.
Packwood said the issue is even more important during the summer, when reliability concerns are heightened amid peak air-conditioning demand in the Southwest.
"Desert Southwest utilities feel they are at risk of an outage, but do not directly benefit from the Intertie," he explained.

The "southern island" members of the WSCC are expected to work out some sort of agreement on the issue before the WSCC study group charged with reviewing the Intertie capacity finalizes a report on spring operations next month.
The WSCC last week approved a winter operating plan for the interstate transmission system allowing an increase to 6,250 MW from 5,200 MW.
The increase is set to take effect this weekend.
But concerns that the winter plan may become obsolete within a short time of implementation have grown as generation and load conditions in the Northwest shift into spring.
Under the plan, the rate of 6,250 MW is in effect until April 30 or until actual operating conditions no longer match specified winter operating conditions.
Those conditions include electricity loads in the Pacific Northwest and power generation at lower Columbia River hydroelectric projects.

In the spring, regional power usage typically wanes as heating demand fades and hydropower generation increases due to the spring snowmelt, which is expected to reach record levels in some parts of the Northwest this year.
"There is some question about whether the winter (Intertie) rate will go up in time to do anything about it," said a source at the Bonneville Power Administration (BPA).

Recent weather forecasts call for above-average precipitation in the Pacific Northwest over the next six to 10 days, with below-normal temperatures in the extreme northwest, above-normal in the southwest portion of the region and near-normal elsewhere.
But WSCC chairman Packwood said recent weather conditions in the upper Columbia and Snake River basins have been "ideal" for regulating the snowmelt.
"It's been 65 to 70 degrees (F) during the day and 25 to 30 at night. The freezing temperatures at night help slow it down," Packwood explained.
The WSCC study group charged with reviewing Intertie operations is expected to meet again April 9 to review spring plans, with a final report expected by April 20.
--D Beasley, Los Angeles bureau + 1 213 955 6761
